edges.effect_quant: A meta-regression of 15 prospective studies found that each 0.01-unit increase in waist-to-hip ratio was associated with a 5% higher cardiovascular-event risk, and the extreme-quantile comparison yielded an RR of 1.95. In 17,232 adults with prediabetes or diabetes but normal BMI, central obesity defined by high waist-to-hip ratio was linked to 54% higher cardiovascular mortality and 43% higher myocardial infarction risk. In a geriatric cohort, waist-to-hip ratio remained independently associated with ischemic heart disease whereas BMI did not.
edges.population: adults being cardiovascular-risk stratified, including older adults and people with dysglycemia or normal-weight central obesity
edges.mechanism: A high waist-to-hip ratio reflects relatively greater abdominal fat deposition for a given body size. That central-fat pattern tracks insulin resistance, inflammatory signaling, and atherogenic lipid handling more closely than BMI alone, which helps explain why cardiovascular risk can remain elevated even in people who are not globally obese by BMI.
edges.summary: The most defensible interpretation is that a high waist-to-hip ratio is a harmful cardiovascular marker even after BMI is taken into account. Across pooled prospective data and later cohort work, fat distribution around the abdomen predicts cardiovascular events more consistently than total body size alone.
edges.caveats: The edge is strongest as a risk-stratification signal, not as proof that waist-to-hip ratio itself is the direct causal agent. Thresholds vary by sex and ancestry, and in some cohorts other central-obesity indices such as waist-to-height ratio perform similarly or slightly better.
